Quietism means a deliberate attitude of stillness, passivity, and withdrawal — a conscious choice to not act, not resist, and not engage with the world around you, but instead to remain inwardly calm and quiet. It is the belief that the best thing you can do — whether in your spiritual life, your philosophical thinking, or even your political life — is to stop doing and simply be still.

The word can be understood at three levels: religious, philosophical, and general.

This is where the word originated and where its meaning is most precise.

Religious quietism is a belief, most strongly expressed in 17th-century Christian mysticism, that the highest form of spiritual life is one of total inner passivity and surrender to God. The quietist believes that a person should completely empty themselves of their own desires, thoughts, and will — and in that emptiness, God fills and acts through them.

The core conviction is this: you should not try. You should not strive for salvation, you should not perform spiritual exercises with personal ambition, you should not even actively pray for specific things. Instead, you should dissolve your own ego and will completely, enter a state of pure receptive stillness, and allow the divine to do everything. Human effort, in this view, actually gets in the way of God.

Think of it like a still pond. If you keep throwing stones into it (your own desires, willpower, thoughts), the surface is always disturbed and you can't see the reflection of the sky clearly. Quietism says: stop throwing stones. Let the water go perfectly still. Then the divine is perfectly reflected.

Key figures associated with religious quietism include the Spanish priest Miguel de Molinos, and the French mystics Jeanne Guyon and Archbishop Fénelon. The Catholic Church eventually condemned this movement as heresy, because taking human effort and will entirely out of the spiritual equation was seen as dangerous — it could lead people to believe that their actions and moral choices no longer mattered at all.

In philosophy, quietism refers to a position that says philosophy itself should stop trying to solve its big traditional problems — and instead just be quiet about them.

Traditional philosophy asks grand, ambitious questions: What is the nature of reality? What is truth? What is knowledge? Philosophical quietists (most famously the philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein) argue that these questions are actually pseudo-problems — they feel deep and important, but they are actually just confusions created by the way we use language. We have tied ourselves in knots with our own words.

The quietist philosopher's job, then, is not to answer these questions but to dissolve them — to show that they were never real questions to begin with, and that once we think more carefully about language and meaning, the puzzles simply disappear. There is nothing to solve; there is only the need to calm down, step back, and see clearly.

In this sense, philosophical quietism is also a form of stillness: instead of building grand theories and systems, the quietist philosopher steps back and lets things be as they are.

Outside of religion and philosophy, quietism is used in a broader sense to describe any attitude or worldview that favors passive acceptance over active engagement — especially in social, moral, or political life.

When someone chooses not to resist injustice, not to protest, not to fight back against problems in the world — and justifies this as wisdom, acceptance, or peace — that can be called quietism. It is the idea that the right response to the world's troubles is to withdraw inwardly rather than act outwardly.

In this general sense, quietism is often used as a criticism. To accuse someone of quietism is to say they are passively accepting things they should be fighting against. For example, a political philosopher might accuse a certain school of thought of quietism if it encourages people to accept social inequality rather than challenge it.

Across all three uses — religious, philosophical, and general — the unifying idea is the same:

Quietism is the deliberate choice of stillness, passivity, and withdrawal over action, effort, and engagement.

Whether it is the mystic who empties the self to receive God, the philosopher who dissolves questions rather than answering them, or the individual who accepts the world rather than trying to change it — all of them are practicing some form of quietism.

It depends entirely on who is using the word and in what context.

From a religious mystic's point of view, quietism is the highest and purest form of devotion — a beautiful surrender of ego to the divine. From the Catholic Church's point of view (historically), it was dangerous and heretical. From a philosopher's point of view, it can be a profound and honest intellectual humility. From a political activist's point of view, it is a failure of moral courage — a comfortable retreat into personal peace while the world suffers.

So the word carries no single moral charge. It simply describes a posture of stillness and non-action, and whether you admire or criticize that posture depends on your values.

• "His response to the crisis was one of quietism — he believed that inner peace was more important than outward protest."
  • "The philosopher was accused of quietism for suggesting that we should stop theorizing about truth altogether."
  • "The mystic's quietism led her to spend hours each day in silent, effortless contemplation."

In short: quietism is the philosophy or practice of becoming still and passive — of choosing not to act, not to strive, and not to engage, but instead to retreat inward and let things be. Whether this is wisdom or avoidance is one of the most interesting questions the word invites you to ask.
